y-m-56-01.title: Can this correspondence be called a function?
y-m-56-01.topic: Meaning of a function: a correspondence in which each input gives exactly one result
y-m-56-01.goal: Test each correspondence against the condition that every input gives exactly one result, sort out which are functions, fix a correspondence that is not a function so that it becomes one, and build a function that satisfies a condition on its range.
y-m-56-01.material:
In a class of 28 students, each student has one attendance number from 1 to 28, and every student has exactly one birthday (ignore leap years). A correspondence in which each input gives exactly one result is called a 'function'. Here, a result means one number (or one attendance number); several results are not counted as a single bundle. There are four correspondences below.
(가) attendance number → the month that student was born (January to December)
(나) month of birth (January to December) → the attendance numbers of the students born in that month
(다) natural number → the number of divisors of that number
(라) natural number → the numbers that are divisors of that number
y-m-56-01.thinking.0: Apply the condition of the definition (one result for each input) to examples and decide
y-m-56-01.thinking.1: Explain with specific numbers why a correspondence is not a function
y-m-56-01.thinking.2: Build different functions that satisfy a condition on the range
y-m-56-01.prereq.0: Middle-school idea of a function (a relationship in which each value of x gives exactly one value of y)
y-m-56-01.prereq.1: Finding the divisors of a natural number
y-m-56-01.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the correspondences that can be called functions.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each correspondence, pick one input and count how many results come out.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.hint.1: Try different inputs and look for an input that gives two or more results, or none at all.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.r.a: This judgment says that each input (attendance number) gives exactly one month of birth. You checked the condition of the definition.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.r.b: If you decided 'there are students, so the number is determined', check whether some month has several students born in it, or no student at all.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.r.c: This judgment says that the 'number' of divisors is a single number for each natural number.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.o.d: (라) natural number → numbers that are divisors
y-m-56-01.s.s1.r.d: A number can have several divisors. Check with a number like 6 whether the condition 'one result for each input' holds.
y-m-56-01.s.s1.explain: In (가), each student has only one birthday, so the month of birth is determined as one month. In (다), each number has exactly one number of divisors. In (나), 28 students are born in 12 months, so there must be a month with two or more students born in it, and the number is not determined as one (there may also be a month with no student). In (라), some numbers such as 6 have several divisors, so the result is not determined as one.
y-m-56-01.s.s2.prompt: The collection of all the numbers that a function's values can take is called the 'range'. For a function f whose domain is {1, 2, 3}, decide the values f(1), f(2), f(3) and make three different functions whose range is exactly {4, 5}. (f(1) is read 'f of 1', f(2) is read 'f of 2', and f(3) is read 'f of 3'.)
y-m-56-01.s.s2.hint.0: First check that the only values you can use for f(1), f(2), f(3) are 4 and 5.
y-m-56-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try making all three values the same and test what the range becomes.
y-m-56-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Some input has a value of f that is not 4 or 5. The range must be {4, 5}.
y-m-56-01.s.s2.fail.c2: One of 4 and 5 never appears. For the range to be all of {4, 5}, both numbers must appear.
y-m-56-01.s.s2.explain: Each input must be given one value, and both 4 and 5 must appear at least once. Of the 2×2×2=8 possible triples of values, remove the 2 where all are 4 or all are 5, which leaves 6.
y-m-56-01.s.s3.prompt: (나) is not a function. Explain why using the numbers 28 students and 12 months, and write one way to change (나) so that it becomes a function.
y-m-56-01.s.s3.hint.0: Fix one month and picture the students born in that month.
y-m-56-01.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine putting 28 students into 12 months, and check whether you can put only one student in each month.
y-m-56-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation clearly mention the case where a month has several numbers or none?
y-m-56-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what role the numbers 28 students and 12 months play in your explanation?
y-m-56-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check yourself that the corrected correspondence gives exactly one result for each input?
y-m-56-01.s.s3.model.0: 28 students are born in 12 months, so there must be a month with two or more students born in it. Then the number matching that month is not determined as one, so it is not a function. If I change the correspondence to 'the number of students born in that month', each month gets exactly one value, so it becomes a function.
y-m-56-01.s.s3.model.1: Some months may have no student and some months may have several, so one month does not get just one number. If I reverse the direction and match each attendance number to the month of birth, it becomes a function like (가).
y-m-56-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: This correction gives the reason from the side of 'a month with no student' and fixes it by changing the direction.

y-m-56-02.title: Where did the equation of the shifted graph go wrong?
y-m-56-02.topic: Translating a graph: checking the equation of the shifted graph
y-m-56-02.goal: When writing the equation after a graph is shifted, do not rely only on a memorized rule for direction and sign; check the equation with a point the shifted graph must pass through, and see that more than one shift can fit a condition.
y-m-56-02.material: The graph of the function y = |x| is a 'V' shape with its vertex at (0, 0), where y = 1 both when x = 1 and when x = −1. (|x| is read 'the absolute value of x'.) Minjae wrote out a solution to find the equation of the graph obtained by shifting this graph 2 to the right (in the positive direction of the x-axis).
y-m-56-02.thinking.0: Check each line of the solution for consistency with the line before it
y-m-56-02.thinking.1: Verify an equation with a point you already know
y-m-56-02.thinking.2: Discover that more than one shift can fit a condition
y-m-56-02.prereq.0: The absolute value sign and the shape of the graph of y = |x| (middle-school level check)
y-m-56-02.prereq.1: Substituting a value of x into a function's equation to find y
y-m-56-02.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minjae's solution that goes wrong.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute the point (2, 0) found in line 2 directly into the equation in line 3.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare each line with the line just before it, one by one.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.line.0: The equation of the original graph is y = |x|, and its vertex is (0, 0).
y-m-56-02.s.s1.line.1: If it is shifted 2 to the right, the vertex moves to (2, 0).
y-m-56-02.s.s1.line.2: It was shifted +2 in the x direction, so replace x in the equation with x + 2 and write y = |x + 2|.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.line.3: So the equation of the shifted graph is y = |x + 2|.
y-m-56-02.s.s1.explain: The first place that goes wrong is line 3. Line 2 says the vertex becomes (2, 0), but if you put x = 2 into the equation y = |x + 2| in line 3, you get y = 4, so it does not pass through (2, 0). Line 4 just carries over the equation from line 3, so it goes wrong too.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.prompt: What is the most direct way to check that Minjae's conclusion is wrong?
y-m-56-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write down which points on the shifted graph you already know.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute that point's coordinates into the equation and check whether the equality holds.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.o.a: Substitute the shifted vertex (2, 0) into the new equation y = |x + 2|
y-m-56-02.s.s2.r.a: You tested whether a point that the shifted graph must pass through satisfies the new equation.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.o.b: Substitute x = 0 into the new equation y = |x + 2| and see whether y = 2
y-m-56-02.s.s2.r.b: You only checked that the calculation works inside the new equation. You did not compare it with a point you already know on the shifted graph.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.o.c: Substitute x = 2 into the original equation y = |x| and see whether y = 2
y-m-56-02.s.s2.r.c: You tested the equation from before the shift. This calculation cannot tell you whether the equation after the shift matches the shifted graph.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.o.d: Accept 'it was shifted by +2, so write +2 in the equation too' as correct and move on
y-m-56-02.s.s2.r.d: You trusted the rule that the sign of the direction and the sign in the equation are the same. Whether the rule is right must be checked with a point.
y-m-56-02.s.s2.explain: If you substitute the point (2, 0), which the shifted graph must pass through, into the new equation, you get y = 4, which shows the mistake. The old equation (a) or a calculation inside the new equation (b) cannot tell you whether it 'matches the shifted graph'.
y-m-56-02.s.s3.prompt: This time, from equations of the form y = |x − h| + 1, make one whose graph passes through the point (0, 4). Find two different values of h. (|x − h| is read 'the absolute value of x minus h'.)
y-m-56-02.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute x = 0, y = 4 into the equation and make an equation in h.
y-m-56-02.s.s3.hint.1: Try a positive and a negative value of h and check whether y becomes 4.
y-m-56-02.s.s3.ok.c1: When x = 0, y = 4, so it passes through the point (0, 4).
y-m-56-02.s.s3.fail.c1: When you put in x = 0, y does not become 4. Put x = 0 into the equation and check it for h.
y-m-56-02.s.s3.explain: Substituting x = 0, y = 4 gives |h| + 1 = 4, that is, |h| = 3, so h = 3 or h = −3. With h = 3 the graph is shifted 3 to the right, and with h = −3 it is shifted 3 to the left, and both are raised up by 1.

y-m-56-03.title: If the range of x changes, does the smallest value change too?
y-m-56-03.topic: Minimum value of a function: how the result changes with the domain (the range of x)
y-m-56-03.goal: Know that even for the same equation, the smallest value can stay the same, change, or not exist at all depending on the range of x (the domain), and build ranges that fit a condition.
y-m-56-03.material: Consider the function f(x) = x² − 4x + 5. (x² is read 'x squared'.) A few values are f(0) = 5, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1, f(3) = 2, f(4) = 5. If no range of x is given, x can be any real number. Let's change the range of x and see what happens to the smallest value (minimum) of f.
y-m-56-03.thinking.0: Keep or correct your judgment to fit new information (the range)
y-m-56-03.thinking.1: Compare the lowest point of the graph with the ends of the range
y-m-56-03.thinking.2: Build ranges that satisfy a condition in several different ways
y-m-56-03.prereq.0: Substituting values into the quadratic expression x² − 4x + 5 and calculating
y-m-56-03.prereq.1: Knowing that the graph of a quadratic function is a U shape opening upward and has a lowest point (grade 9 middle-school level)
y-m-56-03.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.prompt: The range changes at each step. At each step, choose your idea about the minimum value, then decide whether to keep it or correct it after seeing the new information.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first check whether x = 2 is inside the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write the value of f at the two ends of the range next to the value of f at x = 2, and compare them.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Range of x: all real numbers. Among f(0) to f(4) written above, the smallest value is 1 (when x = 2). You have not yet checked whether the value gets smaller at other values of x.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.after: f(x) can be written as (x − 2)² + 1, so 1 at x = 2 is the smallest. At x = 1.5 it is 1.25 and at x = 2.5 it is 1.25, and both are greater than 1.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You only looked at the value at the very end of the table. To find the smallest value you have to compare the whole table.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You picked one value near the middle of the table. Check whether you compared it with the values at other x.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You picked the smallest value in the table. You can check by also trying values like x = 1.5 and 2.5.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There is no minimum value; it keeps getting smaller
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This may be a judgment that missed the shape of the values in the table, which decrease and then increase again.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Now set the range of x to 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 (0 or more and 3 or less).
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the minimum value in this range?
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.after: x = 2 is inside the range 0 to 3, so the minimum value stays 1. Only the largest value has changed (f(0) = 5).
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 2 (the value at the right end, x = 3)
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This may come from thinking that the value at an end of the range is always the smallest. Check whether x = 2 is inside the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: x = 2 is inside the range, so you kept your judgment as it was.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 5 (the value at the left end, x = 0)
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You chose the value at the left end. Compare it with other x inside the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: If there is a range, the minimum value cannot be determined
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment says that once there is a range, the value cannot be determined. Look at whether there is a lowest point inside the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Change the range to 3 ≤ x ≤ 6. For reference, f(6) = 17.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the minimum value in this range?
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.after: x = 2 is no longer in the range, and as x goes from 3 to 6 the value of f keeps getting larger. So the minimum value is at the left end, f(3) = 2.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You corrected your judgment to the value at the left end of the range, x = 3.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You carried over the judgment from the previous step. Check whether x = 2 is in this range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You chose the value at the right end. Look at whether f gets larger or smaller in this range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You may have mixed up the value of x and the value of f. The minimum value is a value of f(x).
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.info: Change the range to 0 < x < 2. 0 and 2 are not included.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the minimum value in this range?
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.after: As x gets closer to 2, f(x) gets endlessly close to 1, but x = 2 is not in the range, so it never becomes 1. Also, there is no x at which you could say the value is the smallest. So there is no minimum value.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You picked a value near x = 0, but 0 is not in the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You used the value at x = 2 as it is. Check whether x = 2 is in the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You picked the value at x = 1. Try values of x that are closer to 2 than 1 is.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: This judgment notices that the value gets endlessly close to 1, but the x that would give 1 is not in the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s1.reflect: The equation stayed the same, but just by changing the range the minimum value was kept (step 2), changed (step 3), or disappeared (step 4). Look back and think about whether the reason you changed your judgment was not the equation but the range (whether x = 2 was inside, whether the endpoints were included).
y-m-56-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose integers p, q (p < q) to make the range p ≤ x ≤ q so that the minimum value of f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 in this range is exactly 2, and find three different pairs (p, q). (Let p and q be integers from −30 to 30.)
y-m-56-03.s.s2.hint.0: First check what the minimum value becomes if x = 2 is in the range.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.hint.1: When x = 2 is outside the range, test at which end of the range the smallest value occurs.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers and p < q.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be integers from −30 to 30, and p must be less than q.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The minimum value in this range is 2.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The minimum value of this range is not 2. Check whether x = 2 is inside the range, and at which end of the range the smallest value occurs.
y-m-56-03.s.s2.explain: If x = 2 is inside the range, the minimum value is 1, so that does not work. If x = 2 is outside the range, the smallest value occurs at the end nearer to 2. If the whole range is to the right of 2, the minimum is 2 when p = 3 (f(3) = 2), and if the whole range is to the left of 2, the minimum is 2 when q = 1 (f(1) = 2). For example, (3, 6), (3, 10), (0, 1), (−2, 1) are all possible.

y-m-56-04.title: Where should point C go to make an isosceles triangle?
y-m-56-04.topic: Distance between two points on a coordinate plane and isosceles triangles
y-m-56-04.goal: Compare the distances between two points using coordinates, build points that make an isosceles triangle in several different kinds of ways, and pick out the case that is not a triangle (all on one line).
y-m-56-04.material: On a coordinate plane there are A(0, 0) and B(4, 0). You want to choose a point C(x, y) whose x-coordinate and y-coordinate are both integers and make triangle ABC. The square of the distance between two points is (difference in horizontal) squared + (difference in vertical) squared. So AB² = 16, AC² = x² + y², BC² = (x − 4)² + y². (Comparing the squares of the lengths gives the same result as comparing the lengths without using square roots.)
y-m-56-04.thinking.0: Turn the condition for isosceles (two sides of equal length) into a comparison of distances
y-m-56-04.thinking.1: Build many different solutions within the constraints
y-m-56-04.thinking.2: Pick out the degenerate case (the case that is not a triangle)
y-m-56-04.prereq.0: Pythagorean theorem (middle-school level): the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose two legs are the horizontal difference and the vertical difference
y-m-56-04.prereq.1: Reading the coordinates of points on a coordinate plane and the meaning of an isosceles triangle
y-m-56-04.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the cases in which triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write down all the ways to pair up two sides among the three sides (AB, AC, BC), which have different names.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the meaning of 'isosceles triangle' in words, and check whether all three sides have to be equal.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.o.a: AB and AC have the same length
y-m-56-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment says that the case where one side AB equals another side AC is also isosceles.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.o.b: All three sides must have the same length
y-m-56-04.s.s1.r.b: If you thought of an isosceles triangle as only an equilateral triangle, picture a triangle where only two sides are equal.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.o.c: AC and BC have the same length
y-m-56-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment says that the case where the two sides other than AB are equal is also isosceles.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.o.d: AB and BC have the same length
y-m-56-04.s.s1.r.d: This judgment says that the side named AB can also be one of the equal sides.
y-m-56-04.s.s1.explain: An isosceles triangle only needs any two of its three sides to have the same length. The three sides do not all have to be equal (that case is an equilateral triangle). So AB = AC, AC = BC and AB = BC are all cases of an isosceles triangle.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose a point C(x, y) where x and y are both integers, y ≠ 0 (because it has to be a triangle), |x| ≤ 10 and |y| ≤ 10, so that triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle. Find four different points C.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write AB², AC², BC² using x and y, then think one by one about which two of them can be equal.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one point, calculate the squares of the three side lengths, and check whether any of them are equal.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.ok.c1: They are integers, y is not 0, and they are within the range.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be integers from −10 to 10, and y must not be 0.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Two sides have the same length, so it is an isosceles triangle.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Among AB, AC and BC there are no two sides of the same length. Calculate the squares of the three side lengths and compare them.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.explain: A point with x = 2 (for example (2, 1), (2, −3)) has AC = BC. For (0, 4) and (0, −4), AC² = 16 = AB², and for (4, 4) and (4, −4), BC² = 16 = AB². If y = 0, then A, B and C are on one line, so it is not a triangle.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Group the points you made with similar ones, and for each group write which two sides have the same length. Also write why you left out points with y = 0.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the x-coordinates of your points side by side.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Explain in words, without a picture, where A, B and C are placed if y = 0.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many kinds your points fall into?
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: For each kind, did you check with equations or numbers which two sides are equal?
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you explain, using the positions of the points, why it is not a triangle when y = 0?
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.model.0: A point with x = 2 is the same distance from A and B, so AC = BC. (0,4) or (4,4) are at distance 4, the same length as AB, so AB = AC or AB = BC. If y = 0 the three points are in a straight line so there is no triangle, so I left those out.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.model.1: If the x-coordinate of C is 2, it is above the middle of A and B, so AC and BC are the same, and if it is a point at distance 4 from the origin or from B, it equals AB. If y is 0, A, B and C are on one line, so they do not make a triangle.
y-m-56-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It is explained in words, but the grouping into kinds is clear.

y-m-56-05.title: Finding a line that meets only at (1, 3)
y-m-56-05.topic: Position of two lines: meeting at only one point
y-m-56-05.goal: Know that whether two lines meet cannot be decided only from the results of trying a few values, tell apart the condition for meeting at only one point (different slopes) from the case where the lines coincide, and build such a line yourself.
y-m-56-05.material: Line L is y = 2x + 1. The point (1, 3) is on this line (putting in x = 1 gives y = 3). Now you want to choose another line M of the form y = mx + n (m and n are integers). First look at which way of judging whether two lines meet is reliable, and then build a line M that meets L only at (1, 3). Think of a line as continuing endlessly in both directions.
y-m-56-05.thinking.0: Compare how valid different ways of judging are
y-m-56-05.thinking.1: Build several lines that satisfy conditions (the point it passes through, the slope)
y-m-56-05.thinking.2: Pick out the coinciding case using a counterexample
y-m-56-05.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope m in the graph of the linear function y = mx + n (middle-school level)
y-m-56-05.prereq.1: Substituting a point's coordinates into the equation to check whether the line passes through it
y-m-56-05.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the ways that let you conclude that the line y = 2x + 1 and the line y = 2x + 5 'do not meet'.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put the same x into both equations and, for a few values of x, write down how the difference of the y values behaves.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the result could be different at an x you did not test, together with the fact that a line continues endlessly.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.o.a: Compare the slopes of the two equations and check that they are equal and the y-intercepts are different
y-m-56-05.s.s1.r.a: This judgment uses the slope and the y-intercept to see whether the two lines lie apart from each other.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.o.b: Put in x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and check that the two y values are never equal
y-m-56-05.s.s1.r.b: You only tested a few values of x. Think about whether there is still a chance they meet at an x you did not test (a decimal, a large number, and so on).
y-m-56-05.s.s1.o.c: Draw the two lines on paper, and if they do not seem to meet, decide they do not meet
y-m-56-05.s.s1.r.c: They may meet outside the part you drew. Check whether you took into account that a line continues endlessly.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.o.d: Check whether the equation 2x + 1 = 2x + 5, made by setting the two equations equal, can be solved
y-m-56-05.s.s1.r.d: This judgment says that if there is an intersection point, there must be an x at which the y of the two equations are equal.
y-m-56-05.s.s1.explain: If the slopes are equal and the y-intercepts are different, the difference of the two y values is a constant 4 at every x, so the lines do not meet. The equation made by setting them equal cannot be solved by any x, which gives the same conclusion. Trying only a few values of x or drawing only part of the lines leaves places you did not test, so it cannot guarantee 'they do not meet' (it can be used to find a counterexample showing that they do meet).
y-m-56-05.s.s2.prompt: Now choose a line M: y = mx + n (m and n are integers from −9 to 9) so that it meets L (y = 2x + 1) only at the point (1, 3). Find three different pairs (m, n).
y-m-56-05.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute the point (1, 3) into y = mx + n and make a relationship between m and n.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put in 2 for m and look at what happens to M and L.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.ok.c1: m and n are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.fail.c1: m and n must be integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.fail.c2: When you put in x = 1, y does not become 3. Check whether M passes through (1, 3).
y-m-56-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The slopes are different, so they meet at only one point, (1, 3).
y-m-56-05.s.s2.fail.c3: If the slope is 2, then an M that passes through (1, 3) coincides with L completely, so the lines do not meet at just one point.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.explain: To pass through (1, 3), m + n = 3. But if m = 2, then n = 1, so M becomes the same line as L and they meet at infinitely many points. So only pairs (m, n) with m ≠ 2 meet at just one point. For example: (0, 3), (1, 2), (−1, 4), (5, −2).
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why m = 2 is not allowed, and say, with a condition attached, whether 'a line M through (1, 3) always meets L at only one point' is always true.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put m = 2 into m + n = 3 to find n, and compare the equation of that line with L.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about whether two lines with different slopes must meet somewhere.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check with a specific equation what line M becomes when m = 2?
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you answer 'is it always true' by attaching a condition (if the slopes are different)?
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the case where the slopes are the same but the point it passes through is different (they do not meet)?
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.model.0: If m=2, the slope is the same, so a line through (1,3) becomes y=2x+1 and coincides with L. Then the lines meet at infinitely many points, not just one. So the slope must not be 2 for them to meet at only one point.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.model.1: Any line through (1,3) whose slope is different from L's meets it at only one point. If the slope is 2, the same as L's, it is L itself, so it does not work.
y-m-56-05.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: This answer is written as a sentence with a condition.

y-m-56-06.title: If two things increase together, is one the cause?
y-m-56-06.topic: Reading relationships in data: two values that change together, and cause
y-m-56-06.goal: In data where two values change together, tell apart what can be said for sure from what cannot, and explain in words a younger sibling can understand why a claim about cause is weak from the data alone.
y-m-56-06.material:
A convenience store wrote down the highest daytime temperature (degrees Celsius) and the number of ice creams sold over eight days.
Day 1: 18 degrees, 22 / Day 2: 21 degrees, 30 / Day 3: 24 degrees, 41 / Day 4: 26 degrees, 52 / Day 5: 28 degrees, 60 / Day 6: 30 degrees, 75 / Day 7: 32 degrees, 83 / Day 8: 34 degrees, 95
Your younger sibling looked at the table and said, "When lots of ice cream is sold, the weather gets hotter. So if the store stops selling ice cream, it will get cooler!"
y-m-56-06.thinking.0: Draw conclusions only within the range the data shows
y-m-56-06.thinking.1: Evaluate the possibility of another explanation (a common cause)
y-m-56-06.thinking.2: Rewrite an explanation to fit the listener
y-m-56-06.prereq.0: Read a table and notice the pattern of two values growing together
y-m-56-06.prereq.1: A rough idea of scatter plots and correlation (middle-school level; no calculation needed)
y-m-56-06.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.prompt: What is the most trustworthy sentence you can say from this table alone?
y-m-56-06.s.s1.hint.0: Follow the temperature column and the sales column from top to bottom and write down how they change together.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each sentence, mark whether it goes beyond 'these eight days' and whether it states a cause for certain.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.r.a: This is the idea that one thing causes the other for certain. The table only shows the pattern of two values changing together.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.r.b: This idea stretches the eight days of data from one store to all stores and all cases.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.o.c: On these eight days, the higher the temperature, the more sales there tended to be
y-m-56-06.s.s1.r.c: This sentence only states the pattern of the two values changing together within the range of the data.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.r.d: This judgment may have missed the pattern of the two columns of the table growing together.
y-m-56-06.s.s1.explain: The table shows that on these eight days at this store, the higher the temperature, the more sales there tended to be (a tendency for sales to be higher on days with higher temperatures). But this table alone cannot say that one of them is the cause, or that it is always so at every store.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.prompt: Instead of your sibling's idea, what new data would give more support to the explanation that 'heat moves both the temperature and the sales together'?
y-m-56-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write down what your sibling's explanation and the explanation 'heat moves both together' predict differently.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether each choice favors one of the two explanations.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.o.a: The number of store clerks was the same two on all eight days
y-m-56-06.s.s2.r.a: The fact that the number of clerks was the same does not help sort out the relationship between temperature and sales.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.o.b: On the same days, pool visitors and electric fan sales also increased
y-m-56-06.s.s2.r.b: This idea gauges a common cause by looking at whether other things related to heat, not the temperature, change together on the same days.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.o.c: The price of ice cream did not change even once during the eight days
y-m-56-06.s.s2.r.c: The fact that the price was the same fits either explanation, so it cannot tell the two explanations apart.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.o.d: The day with the most sales was the eighth day
y-m-56-06.s.s2.r.d: This fact is already in the table, so it is not new evidence.
y-m-56-06.s.s2.explain: If pool visitors or electric fan sales also increased on hot days, that supports the explanation that not only ice cream but several values related to heat move with the temperature. However, this does not prove it is the cause; it only makes one explanation more believable.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain it in 4 to 5 sentences to a first-year middle-school younger sibling. Include what the table does and does not tell us, and your thinking about whether 'the store would make it cooler by not selling ice cream'.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence the pattern that stands out in the table, then write in one sentence what that pattern cannot tell us.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.hint.1: If 'the temperature might come first, or the sales might come first', write one reason for which is more likely.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you change difficult words into easy words so your sibling can follow?
y-m-56-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are specific values from the table (for example the temperature and the sales) in your explanation?
y-m-56-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write 'changes together' and 'is the cause' as different things?
y-m-56-06.s.s3.model.0: Look at the table: as the temperature goes up from 18 degrees to 34 degrees, the sales also go up from 22 to 95. But just because two values change together, we can't say that one of them is the cause. It's more natural to think that it is hot, so people buy more ice cream. So even if the store doesn't sell any, the temperature will stay the same.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.model.1: On these eight days, the hotter the day, the more ice cream was sold. But it's probably not that lots of sales make the weather hotter. If you switch the order, it could be that the weather is hot, so a lot was sold. I think that even if sales are stopped, the temperature won't change.
y-m-56-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is explained in words without numbers, but it reverses the way of thinking.

y-m-56-07.title: The median is 70 points, but the mean is lower?
y-m-56-07.topic: Representative values of data: when the mean and the median differ
y-m-56-07.goal: Check by building score combinations that fit the conditions that the mean and the median can differ, and explain why low scores pull the mean down.
y-m-56-07.material: Five students in a group took a quiz (out of 100 points). All scores are integers from 0 to 100, and from the smallest score in order they are called a, b, c, d, e (a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e). The mean is the sum of the five scores divided by 5, and the median is c, the middle one in order of size. All you heard about the group is this news: "The median is 70 points, and the mean is 62 points or less."
y-m-56-07.thinking.0: Judge what is possible and build counterexamples
y-m-56-07.thinking.2: Compare the properties of representative values
y-m-56-07.prereq.0: The meaning of the mean (sum ÷ number of values) and the median (the middle value in order of size)
y-m-56-07.prereq.1: Arranging numbers in order from smallest
y-m-56-07.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.prompt: What is the most natural way to think about this news?
y-m-56-07.s.s1.hint.0: First write the possible ranges of c, d, e when the median is 70 points.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.hint.1: Put very low values for a and b and calculate the mean.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.o.a: The news is possible if the scores below the middle are very low
y-m-56-07.s.s1.r.a: This judgment says that if the scores lean to one side, the mean and the median can differ.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.o.b: If the median is 70 points, the mean cannot be lower than 70 points
y-m-56-07.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea that the mean is always greater than or equal to the median. Test the case where there are very low scores.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.o.c: If the median is 70 points, the mean must also be near 70 points
y-m-56-07.s.s1.r.c: This is the idea that the middle value and the mean are always similar. Picture a case where the scores lean strongly to one side.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.o.d: For the mean to be low, all five students must be below 70 points
y-m-56-07.s.s1.r.d: This is the idea that for the mean to be low, everyone must be low. If the median is 70 points, check that at least three students scored 70 or more.
y-m-56-07.s.s1.explain: If the median is 70 points, then c = 70 and d and e are 70 or more. If a and b are very low (for example, 0 and 30), the sum becomes small and the mean can be low. So the news is possible.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.prompt: Find five scores a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e that satisfy all the following conditions, and make three different combinations. (Conditions) All are integers from 0 to 100, the median (c) is 70 points, and the mean is 62 points or less.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.hint.0: Put 70 in for c and first put in the smallest values d and e can have.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate how small the sum must be for the mean to be 62 or less, then think about how large the sum of a and b can be.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.fail.c1: All scores must be integers from 0 to 100.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.ok.c2: They are placed in order from the smallest score.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.fail.c2: They are not in the order a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e. Please put them in from the smallest score in turn.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The middle score c is not 70. The median is the middle value when the scores are placed in order.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The mean is 62 points or less.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The mean is greater than 62. Adjust the low scores so that the sum of the five scores divided by 5 is 62 or less.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.explain: Since c = 70 and d, e ≥ 70, d + e ≥ 140. For the sum to be 310 or less (mean 62 or less), a + b ≤ 100 is needed (the smaller d and e are, the more room there is). Example: (20, 60, 70, 72, 80) has sum 302 and mean 60.4. (0, 50, 70, 90, 100) has sum 310 and mean 62.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why the mean is lower than the median in the combination you made, and if you introduced this group with one number, write whether you would want to use the mean or the median, with a reason.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Remove the lowest score from your combination, recalculate the mean, and compare.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count how many people scored 70 or more, and think about which number fits the word 'representative'.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why the mean became lower using specific scores (for example, the lowest score)?
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect both your reason for choosing the median and your reason for choosing the mean to 'what you want to tell people'?
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the one number you chose might misrepresent the group?
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.model.0: One or two low scores pulled the mean down. The median only looks at the middle position, so it stays 70. When introducing the group, most people scored 70 or more, so the median of 70 fits better.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.model.1: The mean adds up all the scores and divides, so it is greatly affected by a very small value like 0 points. The median is affected less by that, so it is good to give both the mean and the median.
y-m-56-07.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: This is an answer that uses both numbers instead of choosing only one.

y-m-56-08.title: Which class uses the class library more?
y-m-56-08.topic: Comparing data: counts and ratios, and the information needed to compare
y-m-56-08.goal: Know that the number of students who used it is not enough to compare how much each class used it, point out the information needed for the comparison (the total number of students), and build the cases that fit a condition when new information is given.
y-m-56-08.material: Last month, 12 students in Class A and 9 students in Class B used the school class library. We do not yet know the total number of students in each class. Here, 'the class that used it more' means 'the class where the ratio of students who used the library to all students in the class is higher'. Remember that each class can have a different number of students.
y-m-56-08.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
y-m-56-08.thinking.1: Sort out the information that is needed from the information that is not
y-m-56-08.prereq.0: Ratio (the size of a part compared with the whole) and comparing the size of fractions
y-m-56-08.prereq.1: A rough idea of relative frequency (frequency ÷ total frequency) (middle-school level)
y-m-56-08.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.prompt: With only the information we have now, which class can we say has the higher usage ratio?
y-m-56-08.s.s1.hint.0: Pick a few possible total numbers of students for the two classes and calculate each ratio.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether which class is higher changes depending on the totals you chose.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.o.a: Class A (because 12 students used it, which is more)
y-m-56-08.s.s1.r.a: This judgment carries the number of users straight over to the size of the ratio. Check whether it still holds when the totals are different.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.o.c: The two classes differ by only 3 students who used it, so the ratios are almost the same
y-m-56-08.s.s1.r.c: This judgment reads the difference in the number of students as the difference in the ratio. Check what happens when the classes have different numbers of students.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.o.d: If we do not know the totals, we cannot tell which class is higher
y-m-56-08.s.s1.r.d: This judgment says that a ratio is a part compared with the whole, so you cannot compare without knowing the whole.
y-m-56-08.s.s1.explain: The ratio is the number of students who used it divided by the total number of students in the class. If you do not know the totals, you cannot tell whether 12 students is the higher ratio. For example, if Class A has 60 students, 12/60 = 0.2, and if Class B has 20 students, 9/20 = 0.45, so Class B is higher, and if Class A has 15 students and Class B has 30 students, Class A is higher.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.hint.0: For the information in each choice, check one by one whether it lets you know 'the total number of students in the class'.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether any of them is not used to find the ratio even if you get the information.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.o.a: The total number of students in each class
y-m-56-08.s.s2.r.a: This judgment says that this is the information that gives the denominator of the ratio directly.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.o.b: The total number of books on the shelves of the class library
y-m-56-08.s.s2.r.b: Check that the size of the library is not used to decide the ratio of students who used it.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.o.c: The average number of times the students who used it borrowed books
y-m-56-08.s.s2.r.c: How often they borrowed is a different standard from 'the ratio of students who used it'.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.o.d: The number of students in each class who did not use it
y-m-56-08.s.s2.r.d: This judgment says that adding it to the number of students who used it gives the total, so you can know the denominator indirectly.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.explain: To find the ratio, you need the total number of students in the class. If you know the number of students who did not use it, you can add the number who used it (12 and 9) to get the total, so it is the same as being given the same information in a different form. The total number of books or the average number of loans is not used in a comparison with this standard.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.acc.0: Choosing only the total number of students in each class is also enough. Also check that the number of students who did not use it, added to 12 and 9, gives the total, so it is the same information.
y-m-56-08.s.s2.acc.1: The number of students who did not use it alone is enough, because it lets you know the total. It is the same as knowing the total number of students directly.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.prompt: You found out that Class B has 25 students in total (9 students used it, so the usage ratio is 9/25 = 0.36). For what total number of students n in Class A is the usage ratio of Class A (12/n) higher than that of Class B? Find three different values of n that satisfy the condition. (12 students in Class A used it, so n is an integer of 12 or more.)
y-m-56-08.s.s3.hint.0: First find, as a decimal, the n at which Class B's ratio 0.36 and Class A's ratio 12/n are equal.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one n, calculate 12/n, and compare it with 0.36.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.var.n: Total number of students n in Class A (students)
y-m-56-08.s.s3.ok.c1: The total of Class A is an integer of 12 or more.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.fail.c1: 12 students used it, so the total must be an integer of 12 or more.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.ok.c2: Class A's usage ratio is higher than Class B's (0.36).
y-m-56-08.s.s3.fail.c2: For this n, 12/n is 0.36 or less. Check what happens to the ratio if the total of Class A is smaller.
y-m-56-08.s.s3.explain: For 12/n > 0.36, n < 33.33…, so n is an integer from 12 to 33. If n = 33, then 12/33 ≈ 0.364, which is just barely higher than Class B, and if n = 34, then 12/34 ≈ 0.353, which is lower. If Class A has 34 or more students, then even though more students used it, Class B has the higher ratio.

y-m-56-09.title: How far can we trust the plant-height line?
y-m-56-09.topic: Showing data with a linear function: the range where a line model is trustworthy
y-m-56-09.goal: Predict nearby values using a line that fits the data, but know that for far-off ranges with no data you must adjust how much you trust the prediction each time new data appears, and explain that judgment in words.
y-m-56-09.material:
We measured the height of one imaginary plant every day (the unit is cm, and the day it was planted is day 0).
Day 0: 5.0, Day 1: 6.1, Day 2: 7.0, Day 3: 8.2, Day 4: 8.9
Thinking that the plant grows about 1 cm a day, we showed it with the line y = 5 + x (x is the day, y is the height). Later data will be given step by step.
y-m-56-09.thinking.0: Compare the model's predictions with new data
y-m-56-09.thinking.1: Decide whether to keep the model or set a limit for it
y-m-56-09.thinking.2: Explain the uncertainty of predictions outside the range
y-m-56-09.prereq.0: The meaning of the linear function y = ax + b and finding y by putting in a value of x (middle-school level)
y-m-56-09.prereq.1: Reading the pattern of change from a table
y-m-56-09.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.prompt: New data comes out at each step. Decide how much to trust the line y = 5 + x.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, calculate the difference between the value the line gives and the value actually measured.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write the range of days that have data next to the range of days you want to predict, and compare them.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The values from day 0 to day 4 all differ by only 0.2 or less from the values the line y = 5 + x gives (5, 6, 7, 8, 9).
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you predict the height on day 5, what would be the most reasonable?
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.after: It is right after the days with data, so the line's value of 10 cm is the most reasonable.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This prediction assumes the growth has stopped. Check whether it fits the pattern of change over the earlier days.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This prediction uses the value the line gives as it is. It continues the pattern of growing about 1 cm each day.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You chose a value that jumps more than the pattern of change. Compare it with the amount of growth each day.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This prediction assumes the height decreases. Check whether it fits the pattern of change over the earlier days.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.info: The height actually measured on day 5 was 10.1 cm.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think about the line y = 5 + x?
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.after: On day 5 the difference is also 0.1 cm, so the line fits the data so far. But this only means it fits up to day 5.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The line fits on day 5 too. We can keep trusting it
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You decided to keep using the line. Check with the next data whether the fact that it fit up to day 5 means it fits for days further away.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The line is wrong. We need to find a new line
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This may be a judgment that saw a 0.1 cm difference as a big error. Measurements can have small differences.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The day 5 measurement is strange, so it should be deleted
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If data fits the model, it is better to leave it as it is.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Do not trust the line; look only at the table
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment throws away the model completely because of a small difference.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.info: On day 10 the measured value came out as 12.4 cm, and on day 20 as 15.0 cm. (The values the line gives are 15 on day 10 and 25 on day 20.)
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: How trustworthy is the 35 cm predicted for day 30 using y = 5 + x?
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.after: The line that fit on days 0 to 5 was far off on day 10 and day 20. So the 35 cm for a distant day is hard to trust, and you have to predict while taking into account the pattern of growth slowing down.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The 35 cm found with the line is the most trustworthy
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment says the line fits even in places that are not days with data. Check the differences on day 10 and day 20.
y-m-56-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The line was off on day 10 and day 20, so 35 cm is hard to trust

y-m-56-09.s.s1.reflect: The line fit well in the range that had data (days 0 to 5), and went off when the new data left that range. With the same equation, you kept it at step 2 and lowered how much you trusted it at step 3. Look back at which data at which step made you change your judgment.
y-m-56-09.s.s2.prompt: You want to tell a friend 'this plant grows 1 cm a day'. Write up to which range of days this statement is right, what data you can base it on, and from where you should be careful.
y-m-56-09.s.s2.hint.0: First write down the days when the line and the actual values fit well.

y-m-56-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid making a flat claim about outside the data, such as 'it will keep going from now on'?
y-m-56-09.s.s2.model.0: In the first 5 days (days 0 to 4), the heights 5.0, 6.1, 7.0, 8.2, 8.9 grew about 1 cm a day. For about that long, it is fine to say it grows 1 cm at a time. But the values on day 10 and day 20 are smaller than the line, so we should not say it is the same after that.
y-m-56-09.s.s2.model.1: For the 5 days measured, it is fine to say 1 cm at a time, but it is hard to say it is so up to a month later. The part with no data may be different, and looking at 15.0 cm on day 20, it seems to be getting slower little by little.
y-m-56-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: It limits the days to 5 days and states the limit.

y-m-56-10.title: Is the parking fee graph a straight line?
y-m-56-10.topic: Graph of a function: a fee that is set for each interval
y-m-56-10.goal: Test a correspondence where the fee depends on time using values from a table, see that the idea 'it goes up by the same amount every minute' is wrong, and describe the shape of the graph in words while building different times that have the same fee.
y-m-56-10.material: This is the fee rule of a parking lot (made up). If the parking time is 30 minutes or less, it is free. If it goes over 30 minutes, you pay 500원 for every 10 minutes over, and a time of less than 10 minutes is counted as 10 minutes (for example, 52 minutes is 22 minutes over, so it is 3 intervals and 1500원). The fee for a day does not go over 3000원. Think of time only in whole minutes. Hyunwoo drew the fee graph as 'a straight line that starts at (30 minutes, 0원) and goes up 50원 per minute'.
y-m-56-10.thinking.0: Test a claim (it is a straight line) with specific values
y-m-56-10.thinking.1: Build different inputs that have the same fee
y-m-56-10.thinking.2: Describe the shape of a graph in words
y-m-56-10.prereq.0: Organizing the values of a function in a table (middle-school level)
y-m-56-10.prereq.1: Knowing that the graphs of direct proportions and linear functions are straight lines
y-m-56-10.prereq.2: This task only shows the difficulty and support level H1 of the generated batch; it does not mean the subject is assigned to a particular grade. Assumption: the basics of middle-school functions, geometry and data have already been learned.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the sentences that fit the fee rule.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the fee for 35 minutes, 36 minutes, 40 minutes and 41 minutes one by one using the rule and write them down.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.hint.1: Test with 100 minutes and 200 minutes how the daily fee limit applies as the time gets longer.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.o.a: Every time the parking time increases by 1 minute, the fee always goes up 50원
y-m-56-10.s.s1.r.a: This idea averages it out: 500원 per 10 minutes means 50원 per minute. Compare the fees for 35 minutes and 36 minutes yourself.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.o.b: The fee for parking 35 minutes and for parking 40 minutes is the same
y-m-56-10.s.s1.r.b: This judgment applies the rule of counting in 10-minute units.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.o.c: Parking 30 minutes is 0원, so parking 31 minutes is also 0원
y-m-56-10.s.s1.r.c: This idea did not check the boundary that free means 30 minutes or less. Look at whether 31 minutes is over 30 minutes.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.o.d: The fee for parking 100 minutes and for parking 200 minutes is the same
y-m-56-10.s.s1.r.d: This judgment checks the case where the daily limit of 3000원 applies.
y-m-56-10.s.s1.explain: 35 minutes is 5 minutes over and 40 minutes is 10 minutes over, so both are 1 interval (500원). For 100 minutes and 200 minutes, the calculation goes over 3000원, but the limit is 3000원, so both are 3000원. It does not go up 50원 every minute (35 minutes and 36 minutes are both 500원), and 31 minutes is over 30 minutes, so it is 500원.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.prompt: Make cases where there are two different parking times t1 < t2 (integers, in minutes) that have the same fee that is not 0원. Find three pairs with different fees (such as one pair with a fee of 500원 and one pair with 1000원). (Keep t2 at 240 or less.)
y-m-56-10.s.s2.hint.0: Use the rule to find the shortest time and the longest time for which the fee is 500원.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.hint.1: Pick two times between those times and calculate whether the fees are the same.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.ok.c1: They are integers over 30 minutes and t1 < t2.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.fail.c1: t1 must be over 30 minutes (the fee must not be 0원), t1 < t2, and t2 must be an integer of 240 or less.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The fees for the two times are the same.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The fees for the two times are different. Check whether they are in the same interval under the rule of counting in 10-minute units.
y-m-56-10.s.s2.explain: The fee is the number of intervals, which is (time over ÷ 10) rounded up, times 500원 (limit 3000원). Two times in the same interval have the same fee: 31 to 40 minutes is 500원, 41 to 50 minutes is 1000원, 51 to 60 minutes is 1500원, and so on, and 81 minutes or more is all 3000원. So there are as many different times with the same fee as you like.
y-m-56-10.s.s3.prompt: Explain why Hyunwoo's straight-line graph is wrong using specific times (minutes) from the fee table, and describe in words what the correct graph would look like.
y-m-56-10.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the fees for 35 minutes and 36 minutes and write how they differ from what Hyunwoo's line gives.
y-m-56-10.s.s3.hint.1: If you drew the graph, write as ranges of time where the fee goes up and where it stays the same.
y-m-56-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation use actual times (minutes) and fees (원) as examples?
y-m-56-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write about the places where the fee suddenly goes up separately from the places where it stays the same for a while?
y-m-56-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also describe the shape after the daily limit of 3000원?
y-m-56-10.s.s3.model.1: It rounds up in 10-minute units, so even if the time increases a little, the fee suddenly goes up, and then it stays the same for the next 10 minutes. It is not a straight line that goes up 50원 every minute in proportion to time.
y-m-56-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer describes the shape of the graph as 'suddenly goes up and then stays the same for a while'.
